'''''The Trials of Oscar Wilde''''', also known as '''''The Man with the Green Carnation''''' and '''''The Green Carnation''''', is a 1960 British [[Drama (film and television)|drama]] film based on the [[libel]] and subsequent criminal cases involving [[Oscar Wilde]] and the [[John Douglas, 9th Marquess of Queensberry|Marquess of Queensberry]]. It was written by [[Ken Hughes]], directed by Hughes, and produced by [[Harold Huth]]. The screenplay was by Ken Hughes and [[Montgomery Hyde]], based on an unperformed play ''The Stringed Lute'' by John Furnell (the pseudonym of Phyllis Macqueen, second wife of [[Basil Cameron]]).<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.richardfordmanuscripts.co.uk/catalogue/23085|title=[ Oscar Wilde; Typescript ] The Stringed Lute. A Play Based on the life of OSCAR WILDE [Playwright's own copy]. WITH Typed Letter Signed P. Macqueen discussing play with W. MacQueen-Pope, theatre historian, revealing pseudonym &#124; Richard Ford|website=www.richardfordmanuscripts.co.uk}}</ref> The film was made by [[Warwick Films]] and released by [[Eros Films]] and has been called the best film ever made by Warwick or Ken Hughes.<ref name="warwick">{{cite magazine|date=8 December 2025|access-date=8 December 2025|first=Stephen|last=Vagg|magazine=Filmink|url=https://www.filmink.com.au/forgotten-british-film-moguls-cubby-broccoli-and-irving-allen/|title=Forgotten British Film Moguls: Cubby Broccoli and Irving Allen}}</ref>

It stars [[Peter Finch]] as Wilde, [[Lionel Jeffries]] as Queensberry, and [[John Fraser (actor)|John Fraser]] as Bosie ([[Lord Alfred Douglas]]) with [[James Mason]], [[Nigel Patrick]], [[Yvonne Mitchell]], [[Maxine Audley]], [[Paul Rogers (actor)|Paul Rogers]] and [[James Booth]].

==Production==
In November 1959, Ken Hughes said he hoped for [[Laurence Olivier]] or [[Alec Guinness]] to play the title role. "I know American actors who would run a mile rather than play a part like this, but the film will be a flop unless Wilde is played by someone of stature," said Hughes. "We are going to have some stiff legal problems. We shall approach the Queensberry family. The Marquis will be shown as the villain and I don't know how his family will like that. As for Wilde, the film will show him deserving pity, a genius living in a superficial fantasy world."<ref name="ken">{{cite news|title=Oscar Wilde's life story to be filmed|first=Edward|last=Goring|date=17 November 1959|newspaper=[[Daily Mail]]|page=1}}</ref>

[[Vyvyan Holland]] (Wilde's son) said "the film company has not approached me. I should be very glad to act as advisor although I cannot say I would approve until I have seen the script".<ref name="ken"/>

In February 1960, it was announced Peter Finch would play the role for a fee of £25,000. "I'm scared stiff," said Finch. "Mind you the fact it's such a challenge is one reason I'm so keen. It's exciting to do something everybody says you can't."<ref>{{cite news|title=Mr Finch signs for Oscar Wilde and £25,000|first=Paul|last=Tanfield|date=16 February 1960|newspaper=[[Daily Mail]]|page=12}}</ref>

The production was filmed in [[Technirama]].<ref name=rival/> The movie was an anomaly among the output of Warwick Productions which specialised in action films.<ref name="warwick"/>

==''Oscar Wilde'' Lawsuits==
It was one of two films about Wilde released in 1960, the other being [[20th Century Fox]]'s ''[[Oscar Wilde (film)|Oscar Wilde]]'' starring Robert Morley. According to production designer [[Ken Adam]], producer [[Irving Allen]] set up four editing rooms for the production, working in parallel during principal photography; this meant that the film could be screened in the [[West End of London|West End]] seven weeks after the start of filming.<ref>[http://www.scriptfactory.co.uk/go/Training/Extract_285.html A Kubrick Masterclass with Sir Ken Adam, Hosted by Sir Christopher Frayling] {{webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20100902131437/http://www.scriptfactory.co.uk/go/Training/Extract_285.html |date=2 September 2010 }}, from [[The Script Factory]]</ref><ref name=rival/>

Warwick took out an injunction against the makers of ''Oscar Wilde'' claiming copyright infringement in two books. The claim was unsuccessful.<ref>{{cite magazine|magazine=Kinematograph Weekly|title='Wilde' injunction plea fails|url=https://archive.org/details/sim_kine-weekly_1960-05-19_516_2746/page/n2/mode/1up?|date=19 May 1960|page=1}}</ref>

==Release==
The film was released at midnight on Saturday, 28 May 1960 at Studio One in London before its general release on 30 May 1960.<ref name=rival>{{cite magazine|magazine=Variety|date=1 June 1960|page=7|title=A Queer Rivalry: 2 'Oscar Wildes'|last=Myers|first=Harold|url=https://archive.org/stream/variety219-1960-06#page/n6/mode/1up|access-date=2 February 2021|via=Internet Archive}}</ref> It was released a week after ''Oscar Wilde''.<ref name=rival/> Producers of both films originally refused to change their movie titles. Eventually, after confusion at various cinemas, Warwick announced they would release ''The Trials of Oscar Wilde'' as ''The Green Carnation''.<ref>{{cite magazine|magazine=Variety|url=https://archive.org/details/variety219-1960-08/page/n275/mode/1up|title=Warwick Gives in on 'Wilde' Title Change|date=31 August 1960|page=20|via=Internet Archive}}</ref>

In June 1960 Warwick announced it would not make films through major studios but would produce and distribute films itself with a slate of pictures worth $8 million a year: "three big films a year" plus eight others which it would finance through Eros (that would cost an estimated $3 million all up). Eros would distribute ''The Trials of Oscar Wilde'' in the UK.<ref>{{cite magazine|magazine=Variety|url=https://archive.org/details/sim_variety_1960-06-29_219_5/page/n2/mode/1up?|date=29 June 1960|title=Broccoli-Allen self-financing|pages=3, 26}}</ref>

In May 1961 Eros ran into financial difficulties, while distributing ''The Trials of Oscar Wilde'' and several staff were fired. Four films were awaiting distribution - ''Johnny Nobody'', ''Middle of Nowhere'', ''Carolina'' and ''Lies My Father Told Me''.<ref>{{cite magazine|magazine=Variety|title=Eros, small Brit indie, runs into money trouble|url=https://archive.org/details/variety-1961-05/page/n198/mode/1up?|date=17 May 1961|page=14}}</ref>

==Reception==
===Critical===
In his review of the film, [[Bosley Crowther]] wrote: "Mr. Wilde himself could not have expected his rare personality or his unfortunate encounters with British justice on a morals charge to have been more sympathetically or affectingly dramatized.  In comparison to that [[Oscar Wilde (film)|other British picture about the same subject]] that opened [in New York City] last week, this one is more impressive in every respect, save one."<ref name="nyt">{{cite news|url=https://movies.nytimes.com/movie/review?res=9C0DE7D7123EEF3ABC4051DFB066838B679EDE|title= Wilde Absolved: Writer's 'Trials' Get New Examination|date=28 June 1960|newspaper=The New York Times|last=Crowther|first=Bosley|authorlink=Bosley Crowther}}</ref> Crowther concludes the review saying "The only thing is you wonder if this is a fairly true account, if Mr. Wilde was as noble and heroic as he is made to appear. And if he was, what was he doing with those cheap and shady young men? It looks to us as if they are trying to whitewash a most unpleasant case, which is one of the more notorious and less ennobling in literary history."<ref name="nyt"/>

[[John Simon (critic)|John Simon]] described ''The Trials of Oscar Wilde'' as "an unjustly neglected movie".<ref>{{cite book |title=John Simon: Something to Declare Twelve Years of Films From Abroad|last1=Simon|first1=John |publisher=Clarkson N. Potter Inc.|year=1983 |page=19}}</ref>

''[[Variety (magazine)|Variety]]'' magazine, commenting on the performances, said "Peter Finch gives a moving and subtle performance as the ill-starred playwright. Before his downfall he gives the man the charm that he undoubtedly had....John Fraser as handsome young Lord Alfred Douglas is suitably vain, selfish, vindictive and petulant and the relationship between the two is more understandable. Where ''Trials'' suffers in comparison with [[Oscar Wilde (film)|the B&W film]] is in the remarkable impact of the libel case court sequence. James Mason never provides the strength and bitter logic necessary for the dramatic cut-and-thrust when Wilde is in the witness box."<ref>{{cite magazine|url=https://archive.org/stream/variety219-1960-06#page/n5/mode/1up|title=Film Reviews: The Trials of Oscar Wilde|author=Rich.|date=1 June 1960|page=6|magazine=Variety|access-date=2 February 2021|via=Internet Archive}}</ref>

The film has been called "Hughes' one undeniable classic."<ref name="filmink">{{cite magazine|magazine=Filmink|first=Stephen|last=Vagg|url=https://www.filmink.com.au/ken-hughes-forgotten-auteur/|title=Ken Hughes Forgotten Auteur|date=14 November 2020}}</ref>

===Box office===
''Kine Weekly'' called it a "money maker" at the British box office in 1960.<ref>{{cite magazine|url=https://archive.org/details/sim_kine-weekly_1960-12-15_523_2776/page/n7/mode/1up|last=Billings|first=Josh|magazine=Kine Weekly|date=15 December 1960|page=9|title=It's Britain 1, 2, 3 again in the 1960 box office stakes}}</ref> The magazine elaborated that the film "did marvelously in good and high class halls but faltered a bit in industrial areas. All the same it's one of the outstanding productions of 1960."<ref>Kin Weekly 15 December 1960 p 10</ref>

==Influence==
The film was the inspiration for a promotional film made for [[the Rolling Stones]] song "[[We Love You]]"; the 1967 film, directed by [[Peter Whitehead (filmmaker)|Peter Whitehead]], featured [[Mick Jagger]] as Wilde, [[Keith Richards]] as the judge in the Wilde trial, and [[Marianne Faithfull]] as [[Lord Alfred Douglas|Bosie]].<ref>[http://www.oscholars.com/TO/Forty-five/Main/editorial.htm Oscar in Popular Culture]{{dead link|date=January 2018 |bot=InternetArchiveBot |fix-attempted=yes }}, from Issue no 45 (July 2008) of The Oscholars</ref>
